{"answer": "The eco-corona/biofilm coats the plastic surface with adsorbed biomolecules and metabolites (proteins, humic/fulvic acids, EPS, lipids, sugars, etc.), effectively masking the native polymer surface and imposing a new outer layer whose own chemistry determines the measured charge (PMC10830523:L132, PMC13057466:L19, PMC13394419:L25). Molecules such as humic and fulvic acids carry multiple carboxylic groups that are negatively charged, so their adsorption shifts the zeta potential more negative, while EPS coatings can reduce or even reverse positive charge on aminated particles depending on EPS molecular weight and concentration (PMC10830523:L132, PMC13057466:L43). This occurs because the corona forms via van der Waals and electrostatic interactions and multilayer adsorption of these charged biomolecules onto the particle, altering the surface functional-group composition and charge distribution rather than the underlying plastic itself (PMC13394419:L26, PMC13394419:L31, PMC10830523:L134)."], "citations": ["PMC10830523:L132", "PMC10830523:L134", "PMC13057466:L19", "PMC13057466:L43", "PMC13394419:L25", "PMC13394419:L26", "PMC13394419:L31"]}

{"answer": "Divalent cations like Ca2+ are more effective than monovalent ions (e.g., Na+) at neutralizing the negative surface charge of plastic particles and compressing/suppressing the electric double layer, which reduces electrostatic repulsion between particles (PMC13213765:L44, PMC11543686:L77, PMC11899741:L77). This charge neutralization and double-layer compression is stronger for divalent ions because the critical coagulation concentration is inversely proportional to the sixth power of ionic charge, making divalent ions 50–83 times more influential than monovalent ions in promoting aggregation (PMC12376886:L46). Additionally, Ca2+ can form cation bridges between negatively charged functional groups (e.g., carboxyl groups) on particle surfaces, further enhancing aggregation and retention compared to Na+ (PMC11899741:L77, PMC9142603:L85). The stronger charge-screening effect of divalent cations relative to monovalent ones also raises the point of zero charge and reduces the effective surface negative charge more than monovalent ions do at the same ionic strength (PMC9142603:L85).", "citations": ["PMC13213765:L44", "PMC11543686:L77", "PMC11899741:L77", "PMC12376886:L46", "PMC9142603:L85"]}

{"answer": "When particles carry a high zeta potential (positive or negative), the resulting electrostatic repulsion between neighboring particles keeps them apart and stabilizes the suspension (PMC12003597:L64; PMC10386368:L45). As the zeta potential approaches zero, this repulsive force weakens, and once attractive forces (e.g., van der Waals) exceed the diminished repulsion, particles are free to collide and stick together (PMC10313666:L27; PMC13488408:L23). This zero-charge condition is sometimes called the isoelectric point, and particles are known to agglomerate at such low zeta potentials (PMC11494166:L27). Consistent with this, studies report that as zeta potential nears zero, particles become easier to aggregate, whereas larger absolute zeta potential values increase aggregation resistance and colloidal stability (PMC8617854:L34; PMC10260929:L35).", "citations": ["PMC12003597:L64", "PMC10386368:L45", "PMC10313666:L27", "PMC13488408:L23", "PMC11494166:L27", "PMC8617854:L34", "PMC10260929:L35"]}

{"answer": "Increasing ionic strength compresses the electrical double layer surrounding a particle, an effect known as electrostatic screening, which reduces the magnitude of the measured zeta potential and electrokinetic response (PMC13298883:L15). This is why low-ionic-strength conditions were deliberately chosen to minimize double-layer compression and thereby maximize the sensitivity and absolute magnitude of zeta potential measurements (PMC13298883:L10). Consistent with this, higher NaCl concentrations were shown to decrease the absolute magnitude of zeta potential shifts even though the qualitative interaction trends persisted (PMC13298883:L16). Similarly, background positively charged ions (Na+ or Ca2+) screen the negative surface charge of particles, reducing the surface negative charge, with divalent ions producing a stronger screening effect than monovalent ions, and via DLVO theory increasing ionic strength compresses the electric double layer and reduces electrostatic repulsion, which is consistent with the reduced zeta potential magnitude observed at high ionic strength for PS-NPs on SiO2 and Al2O3 surfaces (PMC9142603:L85, PMC10450312:L25, PMC10450312:L27).", "citations": ["PMC13298883:L15", "PMC13298883:L10", "PMC13298883:L16", "PMC9142603:L85", "PMC10450312:L25", "PMC10450312:L27"]}

{"answer": "The opposite charges come from the ionizable chemical nature of the added surface groups themselves: carboxyl (-COOH) groups can deprotonate to give a negative charge, while amine (-NH2) groups can protonate to give a positive charge, and zeta potential reflects which of these surface modifications is present (PMC11103427:L23). However, whether an amine-functionalised particle actually reads as positive depends on solution pH relative to the amine's pKa — if pH is below the pKa, protonation is limited, and combined with the intrinsic negative charge of the polymer core (e.g., polystyrene) and possible anion adsorption at amine sites, PS-NH2 can still show a net negative zeta potential rather than positive, as observed for PS-NH2 which had the most negative zeta potential despite amine groups theoretically carrying positive charge (PMC13104249:L17). Thus the sign difference arises from the acid/base chemistry of the -COOH versus -NH2 groups, but the actual measured charge sign is modulated by environmental pH and the polymer core's inherent charge.", "citations": ["PMC11103427:L23", "PMC13104249:L17"]}

{"answer": "Natural organic matter (e.g., humic/fulvic acids, EPS) adsorbs onto particle surfaces, forming an eco-corona that carries its own charged functional groups (such as multiple carboxylic groups on humic/fulvic acids), which alters the measured zeta potential rather than the particle's intrinsic surface chemistry (PMC10830523:L132; PMC7893703:L28). This adsorbed layer can shift the surface charge to be more negative when anionic NOM binds, as seen with environmentally exposed microplastics showing more negative ζ-potential due to humic/fulvic acid coating (PMC10830523:L132). NOM adsorption can also create non-uniform 'patchy' charge distributions on the surface, generating localized heterogeneities in electrostatic potential even when the overall (net) zeta potential does not change dramatically or remains the same sign (PMC13057466:L52). Additionally, coprecipitated NOM (e.g., humic acid with iron oxides) can introduce negative charge and steric shielding that offsets charges from other surface coatings, further modifying measured surface charge (PMC13213765:L56)."], "citations": ["PMC10830523:L132", "PMC7893703:L28", "PMC13057466:L52", "PMC13213765:L56"]}

{"answer": "A protein corona changes the measured zeta potential because proteins adsorb onto the particle surface, altering the surface charge density that is actually being measured rather than the bare polymer surface (PMC4958399:L39). This adsorbed protein layer shields the native (e.g., negative) particle surface charge, and a more robust/thicker hard corona further shields the surface, slowing particle translocation velocity (in TRPS-based measurement) and yielding a smaller zeta potential value (PMC4958399:L42). The degree of shift depends on the specific protein's affinity for the surface, its concentration, and how far the solution pH is from the protein's isoelectric point (which affects how much surface area the protein occupies), as well as temperature, which affects protein adsorption kinetics and corona structure (PMC4958399:L39, PMC4958399:L40). Displacement or exchange of corona proteins over time (hard corona proteins being displaced by higher-affinity proteins, or soft corona proteins dissociating) further shifts the measured zeta potential as protein coverage around the particle changes (PMC4958399:L49).", "citations": ["PMC4958399:L39", "PMC4958399:L42", "PMC4958399:L40", "PMC4958399:L49"]}

{"answer": "UV weathering roughens and fragments the plastic surface and generates oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carbonyl and hydroxyl groups) through oxidative photodegradation, which increases surface polarity, hydrophilicity, and surface charge (PMC8038232:L34; PMC8038232:L19; PMC12030786:L119). This greater density of oxidative functional groups gives UV-aged microplastics a higher capacity to interact with polar species and confers more negative zeta-potential values compared to pristine particles, as seen when aged microplastics (AMPs, -32 mV) were more negative than pristine ones (PMPs, -26 mV) (PMC12030786:L119). Correspondingly, UV-weathering was reported to generally reduce (make more negative) the ζ potentials of microplastics under neutral and alkaline conditions (PMC8038232:L34).", "citations": ["PMC8038232:L34", "PMC8038232:L19", "PMC12030786:L119"]}

{"answer": "Surfactants and dispersants directly change the measured zeta potential because their molecules adsorb onto the particle surface, and the electrical potential measured (zeta potential) reflects the electrokinetic properties of that adsorbed layer rather than the bare polymer surface alone (PMC12637955:L48, PMC10386368:L45). Ionic surfactants can shift the surface charge toward their own head-group charge—e.g., adsorption of the positively charged surfactant CTAB drives the particle charge from negative toward positive as electrostatic attraction dominates adsorption, while nonionic/zwitterionic surfactants like TX-100 or SB3-16 adsorb via hydrophobic interactions and cause smaller or different changes—so the sign and magnitude of the measured potential depends on the surfactant's ionic nature, polarity, and concentration relative to the polymer surface charge (PMC10734291:L62, PMC10734291:L59). More generally, zeta potential is dependent on the dispersant/medium because ions and adsorbed species (including surfactants or serum proteins forming a corona) alter the electrical double layer around the particle, changing the potential at the shear plane that is actually measured (PMC12590796:L11, PMC8719689:L36, PMC10386368:L45). This is why nonionic surfactants such as Tween 20 have been observed to lower the absolute magnitude of zeta potential of particles compared to surfactant-free dispersions (PMC8719689:L36, PMC10340104:L25).", "citations": ["PMC12637955:L48", "PMC10386368:L45", "PMC10734291:L62", "PMC10734291:L59", "PMC12590796:L11", "PMC8719689:L36", "PMC10340104:L25"]}
